full_judgment:
Ashish Ranjan Das J: This Criminal Appeal at the instance of the sole convict Sanjay Kumar Biswas has been directed against the judgment 'of conviction and sentence dated 19-4-2012 passed in Nari-o-Shishu Case No.3 of 2003 arising out of Khoksa Police Station Case No. 3 dated 13-9- 2002 by the learned Judge of the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal, (for short, the tribunal) convicting the appellant under section, 9(1) of Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000 (in brief, Act VIII of 2000) and there under sentencing him to suffer imprisonment for life coupled with a fine of Taka 5,000 in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year more. 

 3. Projected fact of the prosecution that could be gathered from the materials on record succinctly is that the prosecutrix Malati Rani Sharma (for short, Malati) aged about 19 years of a distant village and a daughter of a poor villager used to work in the house hold of Maya Rani Biswas (PW 3) located at College para area of Khoksa town, Police Station Khoksa, District- Kushtia as a domestic aide. While the sole convict appellant Sanjay Kumar Biswas used to be a student of a local college as well as a neighbor to MayaRani Biswas. According to the allegation young Sanjay Kumar Biswas (in short, Sanjay) over the period used to vex Malati Rani Sharma with an intent to establish a secret and illicit physical relationship. But as the Romeo failed in the attempt, on the first date of occurrence ie on 1-2- 2002 in the forenoon he exchanged garlands with Malati Rani and also put vermilion (sindur) on Malati Rani's head saying that by doing this actually Malati Rani's marriage with Sanjay was complete. Next in the afternoon about 6 PM Sanjay all by himself gagging Malati Rani's mouth dragged and in fact abducted her to the dwelling house of the appellant himself located in the same mohulla. He repeatedly promised that he would formally marry Malati Rani in good time. Next by bran- dishing a knife and using force Sanjay committed rape upon Malati in that evening and detained the girl there for the remaining 4 days. During this period Sanjay would commit rape upon Malati every now and then. As Malati was seen missing her mistress Maya Rani notified her father Anukul Sharma (PW 1) living elsewhere. Anukul Sharma came and with the aid of local witnesses some 4 days after the occurrence Malati Rani could be recovered from the dwelling house of this appellant. A time after it was felt that Malati Rani by the time got herself pregnant following the said repeated sexual intercourses with the appellant. The matter was raised with the leading villagers .and the guardians of the appellant. The latters promised that they would accept Malati Rani and give her in marriage with Sanjay formally provided that by the time premarital pregnancy ofMalati Rani is terminated. Thus, on good faith Malati Rani's premarital pregnancy was aborted by administering certain medicine. But the accused party did not keep promise nor Sanjay married Malati Rani. Next Malati Rani raised the matter with the local Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Protirodh committee headed by the Upazilla Nirbahi Officer, Khoksa and in its consequence a salish tookplace on 7-8-2002, but of no avail. In the salish Sanjay was advised to get Malati Rani formally married and as he disagreed he was fined Taka 50,000. In that event also the appellant paid no heed. Thus, having been unsuccessful in the attempt, Malati Ranis father Anukul Sharma filed a detailed written first information report (FIR) stating above with the local Khoksa Police Station late on 13-9-2002 that is, more than seven months after, upon which Khoksa Police Station case No. 3 (69) dated 13-9-2002 attracting section 9(1)/30 of Act VIII of2000 was set on motion nominating Sanjay Kumar Biswasand his parents as accused. During investigation witnesses were examined, Malati Rani's statement was recorded under section 22 of the Act, her physical condition regarding sexual molestation, pregnancy, age etc was examined by a medical board of the Kushtia Sadar Hospital and a certificate to the respect was also collected. After investigation a formal charge sheet was pressed against Sanjay Kumar Biswas alone finding the offence of rape calling for a Penalty under section 9(1) of Act VIII of 2000 prima Jacie proved. Accordingly cognizance was taken by the tribunal, charge was framed to which however the sole accused pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. Next in order to bring the charge home the prosecution produced as many as 7 witnesses including the alleged victim Malati Rani PW 2 herself. Next the accused was examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and in the stage too the appellant stuck to his earlier plea of innocence, but adduced no DW, nor spoke anything positive in defence. 

 4. Malati Rani's father Anukul Sharma as the informant (PW 1) stated his case as he had described in the written FIR (exhibit-1) Prosecutrix Malati Rani deposed as PW 2 describing her case. She added that before filing of the FIR she had brought a petition of complaint before the tribunal that was sent down to the Police Station. She admitted to have earlier made a statement before the Magistrate. PW 3 was Maya Rani Biswas. However she made no statement respecting the happenings of the case. But she was neither cross examined by the defence nor by the prosecution. PW 4 Babul Hossain @ Saheb Ali was a cited witness who denied to have had any sort of personal knowledge regarding the happenings, but admitted to have heard the story from Malati Rani's father. In that stage he was cross examined as a hostile witness by the prosecution as well as by the defence. He denied to have suppressed the truth for some oblique purpose. PW 5 Most Jobaida Khatun used to be the Upazilla Woman Affairs officer, Khoksa. She stated that upon Malati Rani's complain a salish took place presided over by the local Upazilla Nirbahi Officer and its proceeding was reduced to writing with her signature (exhibit-Z, 2/1). PW 6 Dr Abdus Samad used to the Resident Medical Officer of Kushtia General Medical Hospital and he certified that pursuant to police case on 14-9- 2002 Malati Rani was examined by a formal Medical Board and the Board after examination issued a certificate (exhibit -3) and this PW 6 used to be the Chairman of the Medical Board. PW7 Most Umme Salma used to be the Chairperson of the local Mahila Sangstha. But she made no statement in her deposition regarding the case nor she was cross examined. 

 5. Those were all about the prosecution evidences and it requires a mention that neither the Magistrate recording statement of the victim nor the investigation officer could be produced as a witness. The defence plea transpiring from the trend of cross examination of witnesses is that Sanjay Kumar Biswas was absolutely innocent. Maya Rani had kept Malati Rani as her maid servant and had a secret plan to give her in marriage with a suitable neighboring boy Sanjay. But, as the latter's family turned down the proposal, feeling herself insulted and out of vengeance Maya Rani in collaboration with the' Babul Hossain @ Saheb Ali (PW 4) created this case. Neither Sanjay committed rape upon Malati, nor he abducted her, nor Malati Rani was ever pregnant by Sanjay Kumar Biswas. 

 6. The learned Tribunal Court chiefly relied on the evidences of alleged victim girl Malati Rani, her father Anukul Sharma and PW 5 Most Jobaida Khatun taking part in the salish before initiation of this criminal case. The learned tribunal briefly resolved that in such cases of sexual offence hardly there could be a witness available and the guilt of the accused should be concluded upon assessment of verbal evidence of the prosecutrix alone as well as of the attending circumstances. 

 7. Now Mr Sasti Sarker learned lawyer for the appellant submits that in a word there was no legal evidence what so ever that could help conclude guilt of the appellant. There was no witness respecting the fact of vexing Malati Rani by the appellant or of exchanging garlands, putting vermilion, by force abducting her to the residence of the appellant or of committing rape keeping her there for the next 4 days, nor there was a medical evidence respecting any sort of sexual molestation or pregnancy or of its termination. Rather the judgment of conviction has been based on utter surmise and conjecture. The learned advocate particularly raised that although in such a matter the testimony of the prosecutrix is of prime importance, but in the instant case Malati Rani's statement was dubious and absolutely unreliable that could not warrant a punishment. In the matter the appellant chiefly relied on the decision reported in the case of Sahel Rana vs State reported in DLR 205 page 591 and that of Siraj Talukder vs State, 6 BLT High Court Divtsien, 99 page 73. In reply the learned Assistant Attorney General vehemently argued that in such a matter of sexual offence it has been by the time  a settled principle that a conviction may, well base on the solitary testimony of the prosecutrix  alone and in the instant case her evidence was absolutely convincing in bringing the' charge home. 

 9. The fact described in the case may be summarized as follows: 

 Sanjay both by cajoling and using force put vermilion (sindur) on Malati Rani's head and also exchanged garlands. Sanjay assured Malati Rani that her marriage according to the Hindus rituals was thus complete. (3) Next in the afternoon at about 6 PM that day Sanjay all by himself dragged and rather abducted Malati gagging her mouth to his own residence located in a short distance in the same mohulla intervened by a number of houses. (4) Sanjay's house was found vacant and keeping Malati there for some 4 days Sanjay kept on committing rape upon Malati by force. Thus, she became pregnant. (5) By the time the news reached Malati  Rani's father's ear, he rushed with the aid of witnesses, rescued Malati Rani from the house of Sanjoy some 4 days after her abduction. (6) Malati Rani's guardians raised a demand and thus the parents of San jay initially agreed to accept Malati as Sanjay Kumar's wife through a formal legal marriage. But the latter’s finally did not keep their promise. (7) As Malati became pregnant by the time the premarital pregnancy with a hope of formal marriage with Sanjay was therefore amicably terminated by administering some unknown medicine. (8) As the appellant and his guardians were seen rather loathe to keep the promise of a social marriage, a written complaint was registered with the local extra judicial committee headed by the Thana executive, the Upazilla Nirbahi Officer. In the salish as Sanjay disagreed to marry Malati, it was concluded that Sanjay would pay damages or fine of Taka 50,000. But as the accused party disobeyed the resolutions of the salish, some more than seven months after; that is an 13-9-2002 Malati Rani's father Anukul Sharma PW 1 filed a petition of complain that was sent down to the local Khoksa Police Station and this criminal case was set on motion. 

 16. Up to this, these things remained not proved in evidence that (i) prior to the alleged occurrence of abduction and rape, the appellant would vex Malati (PW 2) over a period, with an intent to establish a secret romantic or physical relationship, that (ii) in its furtherance in the forenoon on 1-2-2002 Sanjay exchanged garlands with Malati and put vermilion on her head and thereby assured Malati that her marriage with Sanjay was actually accomplished and that (iii) in the late afternoon on 1-2-2002 Sanjay dragged Malati to his house, gagging her mouth or by using force. But it is the case of the prosecution, as. Malati, PW 2, the prosecutrix claimed repeatedly, that she stayed in the house of Sanjay for quite few days and during the period, understandably, she experienced repeated sessions of sexual intercourse with Sanjay, According to the charge mounted and the verdict of the learned tribunal, the act so done by appellant Sanjay was out and out rape calling for a penalty under section 9(1) of the Act, while, patently, the provision of the offence has been derived from section 375 of the Penal Code of 1860. 

 18. Next, remains the ultimate episode of rape for 4 or 5/6 days as the prosecutrix raised her finger at the appellant. Malati (PW:2) claimed that it was a forceful rape as she had no consent. The learned tribunal believed it and resolved that in such cases a valid conviction may base on the solitary testimony in the matter of the prosecutrix, here PW: 2. Academically, there is nothing to disagree to the principle of solitary testimony in the matter adopted by the learned tribunal. 

 19. But a compulsory precondition attached to reliability of a solitary testimony on any disputed fact, not to speak of that of a prosecutrix is that, such solitary testimony must be absolutely reliable beyond reproach and approach. As a matter of fact the principle of caution has been stressed in a series of cases including that of Sahel Rana vs State, 57 DLR 591 and Seraj Talukdar vs State, 6 BLT (HCD), 1998 page 82 = 3 BLC 182, as the learned advocate for the appellant stressed. 

 21. In its connection, the learned Assistant Attorney General submitted that since by exchanging garlands and putting vermilion on the head of Malati, the appellant pretended to have married Malati. Such a consent, if any, must be, within the 5th proviso of section 375 of the Penal Code, and presumed have been obtained in a fraudulent way. But it has been concluded that there was no reliable evidence of exchange of garlands or putting of vermilion, nor there is a charge of abduction. In that case, the sexual sessions taking place in the house of Sanjay, between Sanjay and Malati, should be presumed to have been amicable and both were adults. Hence, in the matter, the argument of the learned Assistant Attorney General is holding no water. 

 22. Malati in no stage of her statements, given during or before trial, made it clear that Sanjay ever promised to marry her at a particular point of time. Malati before submitting herself to sexual intercourses with Sanjay seems to have been aware that she was yet to be married with Sanjay, as she stated: হিন্দুদের বিবাহ কিভাবে হয়, কিছু ধারণা আছে। That was why, she went out to Panti with Sanjay for the purpose of marriage and next complained with a demand of marriage. Thus, it becomes vivid enough that at the time of submitting herself to sexual intercourse with Sanjay, Malati was aware that she 'Was till that point of time not lawfully or actually married to Sanjay nor there was a specific promise of marriage on a particular future date. In that case her conduct, frame of mind, change of versions at different stages, suppression of facts cumulatively suggest that her lone testimony should not be the only basis of punishment of rape, nor it was safe for the tribunal to rely upon her testimony so far as the issue of using force or of fraudulent means is concerned. 

 23. On record, Malati PW: 2 was adult enough to understand what is marriage, what is premarital sex and what a man can say or how he can behave with an intent to win a girl's consent to premarital sex. In the case of Jayanti Rani Panda vs State of West Bengal, reported in 1984 CriLJ, page 1535, it happened that Jayanti Rani Panda used to be a school teacher. She eveloped a romantic relationship with her colleague-accused. The accused friend promised to marry Jayanti Rani in some indefinite future time and Jayanti continued to maintain a regular physical relationship with her friend-accused. But, as may very often happen, her colleague did not or could not keep his promise. Thus, Jayanti Rani brought a criminal case of rape with a plea that she would not have given consent to sexual intercourses, had her colleague not promised of marriage. Indian Supreme Court acquitted the accused and held that: 

 "The failure to keep the promise at a future uncertain date due to reasons not very clear on the evidence does not always amount to misconception of fact of the inception of the act itself. In order to come within the meaning of misconception of fact, the fact must have an immediate relevance. The matter would have been different if the consent was obtained by creating a belief that they were already married. In such a case the consent could be said to result from misconception of fact. But here the fact alleged is a promise to marry, we do not know when. If a full-grown girl consents to the act of sexual intercourse on a promise of marriage and continues to indulge in such activity until she becomes pregnant, it is an act of promiscuity on her part and not an act induced by misconception of fact. Section 90 of IPC cannot be called in aid in such a case to pardon the act of the girl and fasten criminal liability of the other, unless the court can be assured that from the very inception the accused never really intended to marry her."(Para: 16). 

 24. In the case referred to above, in the matter English view was also discussed, in para 10, as had been observed in the case of R vs Clarence, (1886-90) AER Report: 133. "That consent obtained by fraud is no consent at all, is not true as a general proposition either in fact or in law. If a man meets a woman in the street and knowingly gives her bad money in order to procure her consent to intercourse with him, he obtains her consent by fraud, but it would be childish to say that she did not consent." 

 26. In the case at hand, it finally transpired that fully grown up' woman Malati, on her own volition reached and stayed for quite few days in the house of the appellant. Obviously, while living together with the appellant, 'she indulged in repeated sexual intercourses with the latter and never complained with anyone until she was recovered by her father (PW 1). It may be at best fancied that Malati consented to repeated sexual intercourses with the appellant with a "hope" of future marriage. As has been illustrated above there was no evidence, ocular or circumstantial, of using force by the appellant, nor there is an evidence to conclude that, before indulging in repeated sexual intercourses, the appellant gave specific promise or assurance that he would marry Malati at some particular point of time in future. Hence, it cannot be said that the appellant obtained consent to sexual intercourse from Malati by practising fraud or he had an initial intention to defraud. It is the case of the prosecution that Sanjay's parents disagreed to the marriage and that seems to be the imminent cause that the appellant did not or could not actually marry Malati. In other words, if the statements of Malati (PW 2) made on oath or before, are taken on their face value to be true, then also I cannot help conclude that adult woman Malati, consented to repeated sexual intercourses with the appellant as an outcome of her own mental change, infatuation, attraction towards the appellant and a hope for future marriage. But the learned tribunal ought to have noticed that there was no reliable evidence of deception .meant in 5th proviso of section 375 of the Penal Code of 1860, or of use of force by the appellant before such successive intercourses. Thus, the case of Malati seems to have been fitting with that of Jayanti Rani hinted above. Here two adults, man and woman, indulged in repeated sexual intercourses, where there is no evidence of use of force Or of concrete promise of marriage meaning deception. Two adults, through a complex chemistry of acquaintance may develop a close proximity. In a natural process they come nearer. It may be in our socio-cultural reality, that the female partner initially plays a passive role. But with the passage of time, short or long, the relationship grows further. They assess their mutual profit" and risk factors and consciously or not advances to fulfill their respective hidden desires, physic-mental. In the mysterious journey, they speak and behave keeping in mind their mutual goals that remains in the back of their mind. Slowly, two adults, consciously or not start reaching the body of each other and it goes on and reaches its peak, if not by the time hindered by reasons fountained from a hard reality, as it happened in the case at hand and had happened so in the aforesaid reported case of Jayanti Rani Panda. Only one party of the two contributing to the amicable act' cannot be stamped to have committed an offence of rape and, in my view, the act of the 'male partner should not come within the 5th provision of the Penal Code of 1860, nor it would be fair to bring the act within the ambit of section 9 (l) of the-Act, Rather an affectionate or biased interpretation of section 9 (1) of Act VIII of 2000 tilting towards the adult female partner in one hand, in such cases, may open a flood gate of such embroided and frivolous litigations and on the other hand send an 'improper signal to the society in general and to the female partners in particular that in its turn' help shun their tradition bound values. Here I feel tempted to recall a comment of the aforesaid case of Jayanti Rani that: 

 "If a full grown girl consents to the act of sexual intercourse on a promise of marriage and continues to indulge in such activity until she becomes pregnant, it is an act of promiscuity on her part." 

 27. Here in the case, there was no charge of abduction. The prosecutrix reached the bedroom of the Romeo, on her own accord and stayed there for quite few days. Meanwhile they two came out and once again went back to the refuge of the appellant. Amidst such free mixing, it is presumed that these two adults, man and woman, amicably indulged in sexual intercourses. But, as has been illustrated, the evidence meaning use of force or obtaining consent by deceitful means remained absolutely missing. Hence the charge of rape concluded by the learned tribunal appears misconceived. 

 28. Thus, I agree to the verdict handed down by his lordship of the previous Division Bench of this Court finding the appellant not guilty as I find absolutely convincing merit too in the submission of the learned advocate for the appellant that legal evidences and circumstances in the case were far short from the required standard to rope the appellant with the charge of rape, meant in section 9(1) of the Act. As a result the appeal succeeds, the judgment of conviction and sentence dated 19- 4-2012 passed by the learned Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal, Kushtia, in Nari-o- Shishu Case No.3 of 2002 arising out of Khoksa Police Station Case No. 3 dated 13-9-2002 convicting the appellant Sanjay Kumar Biswas under section 9(1) of Act VIII of 2000 is hereby set aside and the appellant stands accordingly acquitted.
